report:
Conclusion
- The evidence supports a specific, interpretable difference: Model B (B − A positive) pushes the residual stream toward sensational/tabloid, negative/or-offensive lexical content and informal discourse markers — i.e., a stronger tendency to generate “gossipy/clickbaity” and negative/salacious tokens in continuations compared to Model A.

Why I conclude this
- Token-level readouts: the top-voted tokens for the highest-norm cells include many tabloid/gossip and sensational tokens (TMZ, cannibal, binge, scammers, scammers, scammers, payouts, marketers, DJI, Playboy), violent/negative words (graves, hated, deadly, destruction, rifles, slavery), and potentially sexual/medical/offensive tokens (herpes, homosexual, Playboy). Early-layer cells point to discourse markers (“Basically”, “Consider”, “arguments”) while later, high-norm cells point strongly to sensational/content tokens. That pattern reads as a shift in style/topic toward tabloid/sensational and negative content.
- Layer/position concentration: the difference is concentrated in later layers and in positions after the first token (large norms in layers ~11–24, especially positions p1–p4). That localization is consistent with a change that affects high-level generation/continuation choices (style/topic) rather than low-level tokenization artifacts.
- Consistent signals across many cells: the repeated appearance of the same thematic tokens (TMZ, Playboy, scammers, astrolog, Waiter/Summary/Outcome/plaintext/Computation/HDTV) across many high-norm cells and layers indicates a systematic lexical bias rather than random noise.

Caveats / alternative readings
- I can’t prove intent or training objective from this alone. The difference could be a topical bias (Model B more likely to talk about tabloids/scams/gore), a style bias (more sensational or informal phrasing), or a safety-related regression (higher propensity to surface controversial/explicit tokens). The evidence points to a lexical/style/topic shift but doesn’t uniquely identify which training change produced it.
- Patchscope continuations were not shown here; they would help confirm whether the bias shows up as actual gossipy or hateful continuations rather than only shifting logits toward those tokens.

Short answer: Model B exhibits a stronger bias toward sensational/tabloid and negatively-valenced/offensive vocabulary (and more informal/discourse-marking phrasing) than Model A, concentrated in later layers and continuation positions.
